title: California on a Plate, India in the Soul: How Cal-India Cuisine Conquered Silicon Valley
excerpt: The Bay Area duo behind Ettan, Copra and Eylan turned upscale Indian dining into a James Beard contender — and a blueprint for the diaspora's culinary ambitions.
body:
For years the conventional wisdom in American dining was that Indian food belonged at the buffet, not the tasting menu — abundant, cheap and comforting, but rarely the stuff of fine-dining ambition. A husband-and-wife team in the Bay Area has spent the last five years dismantling that idea, one wood-fired, California-grown plate at a time.

## Context & Background

Chef Srijith Gopinathan and restaurateur Ayesha Thapar are the founders of the **Cal-India Collective**, a Bay Area hospitality group whose name captures its entire thesis: Indian flavor, California sensibility. Their first project together, **Ettan**, opened in downtown Palo Alto in 2020 with a contemporary take on Indian cooking that leaned hard on local produce and refined plating. Two years later they added Little Blue Door, a casual concept in a Los Altos food hall. In 2023 came **Copra** in San Francisco, and last year **Eylan** in Menlo Park, a wood-fired Cal-Indian restaurant now listed in the Michelin Guide.

The collective's signature is a "dynamic interpretation of Indian cuisine that feels bright, vibrant, and rooted in California," as Gopinathan has described it — spice and technique from the subcontinent, ingredients and lightness from the West Coast.

## Current Developments

That vision earned the pair national recognition. Gopinathan and Thapar were named finalists for the **2026 James Beard Award for Outstanding Restaurateur**, one of only five teams in the country — and the only Peninsula nominee — to make the cut for the category, which honors industry leaders who build community through their restaurants.

While the top medal in their category ultimately went to Maine's Dana Street at the June 15 ceremony in Chicago, the nomination itself was a milestone. It placed an Indian-American hospitality group alongside the most celebrated restaurateurs in America, and underscored a broader surge of Indian talent at the awards — from Asheville's Chai Pani group to a wave of Michelin-recognized regional Indian restaurants opening across US metros.

## Diaspora Impact

For Indian Americans, especially the large, affluent South Asian community of the Bay Area, Cal-India's rise is deeply personal. It signals that the food of home can occupy the same rarefied space as French or Japanese cuisine — that a dosa or a wood-fired kebab can be plated with the same intention as anything at a three-star tasting menu, and command the same respect and price.

It also reflects the diaspora's own evolution. The second and third generations who grew up on weekend dal-chawal now have the spending power and confidence to seek out elevated versions of their heritage cuisine, not as novelty but as a source of pride. Restaurants like Ettan and Eylan give them a place to take colleagues and dates and feel that their culture is being honored, not flattened.

The collective's success also rewrites the economics of Indian dining in America. Where the old model relied on high volume and low margins — the all-you-can-eat lunch buffet — Cal-India's restaurants command tasting-menu prices and the kind of investor attention once reserved for European or Japanese concepts. That shift gives a new generation of Indian-American chefs permission to be ambitious, to source heirloom produce, to plate with intention, and to charge accordingly. Gopinathan's own path — from luxury hotel kitchens to a Michelin-listed wood-fired room in Menlo Park — has become a template that aspiring desi restaurateurs now study closely.

## What's Next

The Beard recognition tends to bring a measurable "Beard bump" — more reservations, more press, more investor interest. For the Cal-India Collective, that could mean further expansion across the Peninsula and beyond. More broadly, the moment marks a turning point: Indian fine dining in America is no longer a curiosity but a category, with its own stars, its own grammar, and a growing diaspora audience ready to fill the tables.
